Enhanced anaerobic digestion performance and sludge filterability by 
membrane microaeration for anaerobic membrane bioreactor application 
Chun-Hai Wei a,b,1,*, Zheng-Wei Wang a,1, Jian-Hua Dai a, Kang Xiao c, Hua-Rong Yu a,b,

A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Membrane fouling potential 
Methanogenesis 
Oxidation-reduction potential 
Particle size distribution 
Volatile fatty acid 
A B S T R A C T   
Slow dissolution/hydrolysis of insoluble/macromolecular organics and poor sludge filterability restrict the 
application potential of anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR). Bubble-free membrane microaeration was 
firstly proposed to overcome these obstacles in this study. The batch anaerobic digestion tests feeding insoluble 
starch and soluble peptone with and without microaeration showed that microaeration led to a 65.7–144.8% 
increase in methane production and increased critical flux of microfiltration membrane via driving the formation 
of large sludge flocs and the resultant improvement of sludge settleability. The metagenomic and bioinformatic 
analyses showed that microaeration significantly enriched the functional genes and bacteria for polysaccharide 
and protein hydrolysis, microaeration showed little negative effects on the functional genes involved in anaer­
obic metabolisms, and substrate transfer from starch to peptone significantly affected the functional genes and 
microbial community. This study demonstrates the dual synergism of microaeration to enhance the dissolution/ 
hydrolysis/acidification of insoluble/macromolecular organics and sludge filterability for AnMBR application.

1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is promising to treat high-strength organic 
wastewater and solid waste for organics removal and methane recovery 
(Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a). However, high-concentration 
insoluble organics in some wastewaters (e.g., livestock wastewater) and 
solid wastes (e.g., excess sludge) usually take long time (20–30 d) for 
sequential dissolution/hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and 
methanogenesis in conventional completely mixed AD process. Anaer­
obic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) coupling anaerobic activated 
sludge degradation and micro/ultra-filtration membrane separation can 
achieve complete separation of hydraulic and sludge retention time and 
partial separation of hydraulic and macromolecular organics retention 
time via high-efficiency membrane rejection, being an advanced process 
suitable for treating wastewater containing high-concentration insol­
uble organics (Ying et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2016). However, AnMBR is 
still facing the challenges including slow dissolution/hydrolysis rate of 
insoluble organics, sensitive methanogenic activity and membrane 
fouling caused by poor anaerobic sludge filterability (Song et al., 2018). 
Microaeration (i.e., injecting or in-situ chemically/electrochemically 
generating trace oxygen) has been considered as an effective strategy to 
enhance hydrolysis in AD and remove hydrogen sulfide from biogas in 
recent years (Hu et al., 2017). The trace oxygen typically at 0.005–1 L 
O2/L reactor/day into AD system would be rapidly consumed by 
facultative bacteria (Nguyen & Khanal, 2018), which could not only 
stimulate the secretion of extracellular enzymes and thus promote the 
dissolution/hydrolysis of insoluble/macromolecular organics, but also 
protect methanogens from oxygen stress and thus avoid negative effects 
on methanogenesis (Fu et al., 2022). Several studies (Amin et al., 2021; 
Cao et al., 2022; Iftikhar et al., 2021) evaluated microaeration-assisted 
AD for swine/cattle manure and cellulose treatment and showed that 
microaeration effectively improved the dissolution/hydrolysis effi­
ciency of insoluble organics and finally enhanced methane production. 
Microaeration may facilitate some microorganisms with a unique cyto­
chrome bd oxidase to achieve nanaerobic respiration at very low dis­
solved oxygen (<2 μM), where simple organics (e.g., glucose, butyrate, 
propionate, acetate) can be directly oxidized to carbon dioxide (Wu 
et al., 2020). Hydrogenotrophic methanogens can further convert these 
carbon dioxide and hydrogen derived from acidogenesis and aceto­
genesis into methane (Wu et al., 2023). Microaeration has also some 
advantages of simple operation and low cost over other reported oxygen 
supply methods for AD including in-situ slow oxygen release via dosing 
calcium peroxide (Fu et al., 2018) and in-situ oxygen supply via water 
electrolysis (Tartakovsky et al., 2011), thus promoting its real 
application. 
Microaeration in AD may induce the formation of stratified flocs with 
a core of strict anaerobes (e.g., methanogens) and an outer layer of 
facultative bacteria, where the outer layer of facultative bacteria pro­
tects the oxygen-sensitive anaerobes by scavenging reactive oxygen 
species through aerobic metabolism (Liu et al., 2009; Nguyen & Khanal, 
2018). This may also affect the secretion of extracellular polymeric 
substances (EPS) and induce the formation of larger flocs, which further 
affect the settleability and dewaterability of anaerobic sludge (Stewart & 
Franklin, 2008). This was confirmed in a recent study (Zhou et al., 
2021), which found that in situ microaeration (aeration of 12.5 mL/L/d) 
not only increased methane production and volatile solids removal, but 
also effectively increased sludge particle size and improved its dew­
aterability via reducing the ratio of loosely-bounded EPS to tightly- 
bounded EPS. In addition, the formation of large microbial aggregates 
with outer facultative bacteria and inner methanogens may not only 
facilitate the potential syntrophic interactions between bacteria and 
methanogens, but also improve its settleability and thus mitigate the 
potential membrane fouling in AnMBR application (Cheng et al., 2018). 
Although microaeration has shown the abovementioned advantages 
for AD treatment of high-concentration insoluble organic wastewater 
and solid waste, some drawbacks still hinder its wide application (Aslam 
et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2022), for example, how to achieve uniform 
aeration, improve the oxygen transfer rate and achieve the high- 
efficiency synergy between microaeration and methanogenesis is a key 
consideration (Chen et al., 2019). Bubble-free membrane microaeration 
can directly supply molecular oxygen into anaerobic sludge mixture and 
thus eliminates the gas-to-liquid mass transfer resistance, which has 
been used to achieve more uniform aeration and enhance refractory 
compound’s hydrolysis (Zhang et al. 2022a). Therefore, a new AnMBR 
prototype assisted with membrane microaeration was proposed for the 
first time in this study. Sequential batch AD tests without, with, and 
without oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) controlled microaeration 
were conducted using two substrates (insoluble starch and soluble 
peptone), where organics degradation, methane production and mi­
crobial metagenomic characteristics were monitored in order to clarify 
the performance and mechanism of microaeration on AD of insoluble 
and macromolecular organics (see supplementary materials). At the end 
of each batch AD test, both critical flux evaluation of the microfiltration 
membrane and sludge characterization (suspended solids fractionation 
and particle size distribution) were conducted to reveal the performance 
and mechanism of microaeration on sludge filterability. The outcomes of 
this study would provide new insights into the potential double en­
hancements for AnMBR application by microaeration. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Reactor and raw anaerobic sludge 
The AnMBR prototype used in this study (see supplementary mate­
rials) consisted of a completely mixing anaerobic bioreactor with an 
effective volume of 22.5 L, a submerged polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) 
hollow fiber microfiltration membrane module with an effective filtra­
tion area of 0.34 m2 and nominal pore size of 0.1 μm (Beijing Origin 
Water, China), a ZeeLung selective oxygen permeable bubble-free 
aeration hollow fiber membrane module with an effective area of 
0.25 m2 (Veolia, France, see supplementary materials), a peristaltic 
suction pump for membrane permeating, a biogas circulation pump 
supplying biogas at a recirculation rate of 15 L/min via a perforated tube 
to the bottom of two membrane modules and thus creating well-mixing 
in the reactor and scouring on membrane surface, a microaeration pump 
with pressure adjustment (0–5 kPa) depending on ORP to deliver air into 
the lumen of hollow fiber aeration membrane, pressure gauges for 
monitoring suction pressure of microfiltration membrane and air supply 
pressure of microaeration membrane, and a AMPTS II fully automatic 
methane potential testing system for recording methane production 
(Bioprocess Control, Sweden, see supplementary materials). The 
anaerobic activated sludge in the reactor had been well acclimated to 
and grew with the soluble starch (i.e., dissolving the insoluble starch 
mentioned below in hot water of 70 ◦C) as carbon source during a 6- 
month AnMBR operation prior to this study and its characteristics at 
the beginning of this study were described (see supplementary 
materials). 
2.2. Batch AD tests 
Sequential batch AD tests without microaeration (AD1) → with 
microaeration (AD2) → with microaeration (AD3) and without 
microaeration (AD4) → with microaeration (AD5) → with microaeration 
(AD6) were conducted using two representative carbon sources −
insoluble starch and soluble bacterial peptone prepared by enzymatic 
digestion of selected animal tissues (i.e., a mixture of proteins, peptides 
and amino acids), respectively (see supplementary materials). At the 
start of each AD test, the concentrated stock of insoluble starch or sol­
uble peptone was directly injected into the bioreactor to reach the target 
dosage of 4 g/L for chemical oxygen demand (COD), NH4Cl and 
Na2HPO4 in the concentrate stock were used as nitrogen and phosphorus 
sources to ensure the target COD:N:P of 200:5:1 for the added substrates,

NaHCO3 in the concentrate stock was also dosed at 4 g/L (i.e., equivalent 
to COD) as a buffer to avoid the large fluctuation of pH in the bioreactor. 
At the end of each AD test, the supernatant was discharged via micro­
filtration membrane permeation to make the effective volume as the 
same with before injecting the concentrated stock. In order to avoid any 
oxygen intrusion for AD tests without microaeration, nitrogen stripping 
via the perforated tube was conducted to flush the system immediately 
after injecting the concentrated stock. The ORP was controlled in the 
range of −150 to −100 mV via adjusting the output of microaeration 
pump in AD2 and AD5, while it was in the range of −400 to −300 mV in 
other AD tests without microaeration. The pH was in the range of 
6.7–8.1 during all AD tests without extra acid/alkali dosage for pH 
control. All AD tests were conducted in room temperature of 20–22 ◦C. 
During each batch test, sludge sample of 10 ml was taken daily and pre- 
filtrated via 0.45 μm membrane syringe filter for water quality deter­
mination. In addition, the half of anaerobic sludge in the bioreactor was 
taken out for seeding another reactor after AD3 and the same amount of 
tap water was filled to the bioreactor before AD4, thus resulting in the 
much lower initial COD in AD4-6 than AD1-3. Methane production 
without microaeration was directly measured by AMPTS II, while 
methane production with microaeration was collected via gas bag and 
measured by gas chromatography (Techcomp, GC7900, China) to 
eliminate the effect of entrapped nitrogen via membrane microaeration 
(Amin et al., 2021). Each batch test was operated till no methane 
production. 
2.3. Sludge filterability tests via critical flux determination 
At the end of each AD test, the critical flux of microfiltration mem­
brane was measured via the classical flux stepwise increment method­
ology (Fox & Stuckey, 2015; Le Clech et al. 2003b), where 
transmembrane pressure (TMP) as membrane fouling indicator was 
continuously measured with time under each constant flux and TMP 
increasing rate was employed to determine critical flux zone. Membrane 
permeate was returned into the bioreactor and the same peristaltic 
pump speed was employed during filtration test to make the results 
comparable among different AD tests in this study. During critical flux 
determination, a 15 min idle interval for the microfiltration membrane 
without permeation was employed between two constant-flux filtration 
tests in order to remove the deposited particles on membrane surface via 
biogas scouring. During AD tests, the microfiltration membrane without 
permeation was always under biogas scouring condition. Sludge was 
also sampled for solids characterization in terms of easy/difficult set­
tleability and particle size distribution to clarify the potential mecha­
nism behind the critical flux changes without and with microaeration.

2.4. Physicochemical analyses 
Sludge samples were directly measured for total solids (TS), sus­
pended solids (SS), volatile suspended solids (VSS), and total chemical 
oxygen demand (TCOD) according to the standard methods (Federation 
& Association, 2005). Sludge samples were separated by centrifugation 
at 3000 g for 10 min into pellet (i.e., easy-to-settle SS) and supernatant 
(i.e., difficult-to-settle SS). The laser particle size analyzer (BT-9300S, 
Dandong Baite Instrument Co., Ltd, China) was used to measure particle 
size distribution of sludge mixtures (including original sludge, pellet, 
and supernatant) based on dynamic light scattering method. The su­
pernatant samples were further separated by 0.45 μm membrane syringe 
filter to produce water samples. The water samples were measured for 
soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) via the standard methods 
(Federation & Association, 2005), for proteins via the Bradford method, 
for amino acids via the ninhydrin colorimetric method, for poly­
saccharides via the phenol–sulphuric acid method, for volatile fatty 
acids (VFAs) via gas chromatography (Techcomp, GC7980, China), and 
for fluorescent substances via the three-dimensional fluorescence spec­
trometry (Shimadzu-RF-6000, Japan), respectively. 
2.5. Metagenomics analyses 
Metagenome sequencing and bioinformatics analysis were employed 
to investigate microbial communities and critical function genes related 
to AD via the Majorbio Platform (Zhang et al., 2019). The sludge mixture 
was firstly concentrated by centrifugation (4000 g, 5 min) to obtain a 
microbial-rich pellet sample for testing, which was stored at −80 ◦C 
pending delivery. Three samples from raw sludge before AD tests 
(notated as Sludge-Blank), starch-feeding sludge at the end of AD2 with 
microaeration (notated as Sludge-Starch), and peptone-feeding sludge at 
the end of AD5 with microaeration (noted as Sludge-Peptone) were 
obtained for the metagenome sequencing analysis. The brief process 
included: 1) Total genomic DNA was extracted from the samples using 
the E.Z.N.A.® Soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, U.S.); 2) DNA 
extract quality was checked on 1 % agarose gel; 3) Fragmentation of 
samples (~400 bp) was conducted using ultrasound (Covaris M220, 
USA); 4) Sequencing library was constructed using the NEXTflex Rapid 
DNA-Seq; 5) Sequencing was finally conducted via the Illumina Nova­
Seq/Hiseq Xten (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) by Majorbio Bio- 
Pharm Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Raw data for genome 
sequencing was processed on a free online platform at Majorbio Cloud 
(cloud.majorbio.com). Species metabolic pathway-related genes were 
obtained from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) 
database (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/). 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of microaeration on AD performance 
3.1.1. Organics removal and methane recovery 
Fig. 1a, d, and f shows the soluble polysaccharide, TCOD/SCOD, and 
methane production with reaction time for the starch-feeding groups (i. 
e., AD 1–3), respectively. From the Fig. 1a, soluble polysaccharides 
showed an initial increase followed by decrease with reaction time, 
indicating the dissolution of the injected insoluble starch and subse­
quent utilization by hydrolytic bacteria. There was a 67.7–104 % higher 
initial increase and 244.5–307 % higher subsequent decrease of soluble 
polysaccharides in AD2 with microaeration than in AD1 and AD3 
without microaeration, showing the significantly enhanced dissolution/ 
hydrolysis by microaeration, which was consistent with previous studies 
(Hu et al., 2017; Zhang et al. 2022b). From Fig. 1d, TCOD showed a 
gradual decrease while SCOD showed small fluctuations with reaction 
time, indicating that the insoluble starch was the main contributor of 
TCOD removal and the dissolution of insoluble starch was the key rate- 
limiting step for its anaerobic degradation. There was a 80.7–125.8 % 
higher TCOD removal in AD2 with microaeration than in AD1 and AD3 
without microaeration, showing the significantly enhanced insoluble 
starch removal by microaeration. From Fig. 1f, methane production 
showed a lag period of 4 and 3 d for AD1 and AD3 without microaera­
tion, respectively, which could be derived from slow dissolution of 
insoluble starch. Then, methane production showed a rapid increase till 
7 d followed by a slow increase to 292.6 and 324.9 ml at the end of AD1 
and AD3, respectively. In AD2 with microaeration, methane production 
showed a rapid increase till 6 d followed by a slow increase to a final 
716 ml. No lag period for methane production and a 144.7 % and 120.4 
% higher methane production in AD2 with microaeration than AD1 and 
AD3 without microaeration demonstrated that microaeration did not 
inhibit methanogenesis but on the contrary promoted methanogenesis 
via enhancing the dissolution/hydrolysis of insoluble starch in this 
study, which was consistent with previous studies (Hu et al., 2017; 
Zhang et al. 2022b). 
Fig. 1b, c, e, and g shows protein, amino acid, COD, and methane 
production with reaction time for the peptone-feeding groups (i.e., AD 
4–6), respectively. From Fig. 1b, there was an initial protein increase 
followed by a slow protein decrease with reaction time in AD4 and AD6 
without microaeration, indicating the possible initial microbial secre­
tion of endogenous protein in terms of soluble microbial products and 
the following protein hydrolysis with reaction time. There was a 
35.2–39.4 % higher initial protein in AD5 with microaeration than AD4 
and AD6 without microaeration, implying that microaeration

significantly enhanced the secretion of endogenous protein. In addition, 
there was a 108 %-255.6 % higher protein removal in AD5 with 
microaeration than AD4 and AD6 without microaeration, indicating the 
significantly enhanced protein removal by microaeration (Zhang et al., 
2021b). From Fig. 1c, there was a 9.9 % higher initial increase and 
318.4–401.7 % higher subsequent decrease of amino acid with reaction 
time in AD5 than in AD4 and AD6, showing the enhanced protein hy­
drolysis and amino acid utilization by microaeration. From Fig. 1e, there 
was a slow decrease of TCOD and SCOD with reaction time, and TCOD 
removal increased by 58.5 %-63 % in AD5 with microaeration than in 
AD4 and AD6 without microaeration, indicating the significantly 
enhanced protein mineralization by microaeration. From Fig. 1g, 
methane production without lag period showed an initial rapid increase 
followed by slow increase to the final 289.7 ml, 515.1 ml, 310.9 ml in 
AD4, AD5, AD6, respectively. Significantly faster and a 77.8 % and 65.7 
% higher methane production in AD5 with microaeration than in AD4 
and AD6 without microaeration demonstrated that microaeration did 
not inhibit methanogenesis but on the contrary promoted methano­
genesis via enhancing protein hydrolysis and subsequent amino acid 
utilization in this study. The rapid methane production from the 1st to 
2nd day could be derived from the consumption of peptides, while the 
changes in protein and amino acid with reaction time might be affected 
by the secretion of endogenous soluble microbial products from micro­
bial metabolism and their decrease after the rapid methane production 
might be ascribed into microbial cell anabolism rather than methane 
production catabolism. In addition, from fluorescence analysis (see 
supplementary materials), the intensity of the protein peaks decreased 
from the start to the end of AD test significantly in AD5, but not in AD4, 
and decreased slightly in AD6, which were similar to the results for 
protein and amino acid, demonstrating the enhanced hydrolysis of 
protein-like substances by microaeration. 
3.1.2. Residual VFAs distribution 
Fig. 2a and b shows the VFAs concentration at the end of AD tests 
with starch and peptone feeding, respectively. From Fig. 2a for starch- 
feeding groups, AD2 with microaeration contained only 10.6 mg/L of 
acetic acid, while AD1 and AD3 without microaeration contained pro­
pionic acid (503.3 and 391.3 mg/L) and butyric acid (83.6 and 151.9 
mg/L), respectively. From Fig. 2b for peptone-feeding groups, AD5 with 
microaeration contained higher concentration of acetic acid (265.3 mg/ 
L), while AD4 and AD6 without microaeration contained higher con­
centration of propionic acid (650.6 and 333.9 mg/L, respectively). 
Acetic acid seemed to dominate under microaeration conditions, and it 
could be consumed more rapidly by methanogens. Propionic acid 
appeared to be more abundant without microaeration conditions, which 
might be a result of the high abundance of Propionibacterium (a fast 
growing and producing propionic acid species under exclusively 
anaerobic conditions) (Sawatdeenarunat et al., 2017). Propionic acid 
metabolism was known to be thermodynamically unfavorable, while 
microaeration seemed to avoid propionic acid production via inhibiting

Propionibacterium (Xu et al., 2020). Therefore, microaeration could not 
only enhance the dissolution/hydrolysis of organics, but also greatly 
reduce the accumulation of propionate and promoted the rapid con­

3.2. Effect of microaeration on anaerobic sludge filterability 
3.2.1. Critical flux of microfiltration membrane 
Fig. 3 presents the critical flux measurement results of anaerobic 
sludge at the end of AD tests. From Fig. 3a and b showing TMP increase 
with time during critical flux measurement of starch-feeding group, TMP 
increase rate with time was linearly fitted as 0.0886, 0.124, 0.5301 kPa/ 
min and 0.0349, 0.0819, 0.8368 kPa/min under the constant flux of 
1.47, 2.47, 3.44 L/m2/h (LMH) for no microaeration and microaeration, 
respectively, indicating a significant improvement of critical flux and 
anaerobic sludge filterability. From Fig. 3c and d showing TMP increase 
with time during critical flux measurement of peptone −feeding group, 
TMP increase rate with time was linearly fitted as 0.0085, 0.1929, 
0.2679 kPa/min and 0.0041, 0.0709, 0.3543 kPa/min under the con­
stant flux of 1.76, 2.71, 3.53 LMH for no microaeration and microaer­
ation, respectively. It should be pointed out that some correlation 
coefficients of linear fitting between TMP and filtration time were not so 
good (e.g., R2 < 0.95) from Fig. 3. This was mainly due to the complex 
nature of membrane fouling occurred during a short-term constant-flux 
filtration of anaerobic sludge (e.g., pore blocking may happen and thus 
result in that cake/gel layer might not be the dominant fouling 
mechanism). 
For the field of membrane bioreactor with complex sludge mixture 
(consisting of sludge flocs, colloids, and soluble substances in a large size 
range of 10-3 to 103 μm) to be filtrated, the critical flux is generally 
regarded as the one, below which no or little TMP increase during a 
short-term (e.g., 0.5–2 h) constant-flux filtration test (Le Clech et al. 
2003a). However, the TMP increasing rate under critical flux has not an 
accepted standard so far. That’s why there are different TMP increasing 
rate employed to determine critical flux in the literature (De Vela, 
2021). Taking TMP increase rate of 0.1 kPa/min as critical flux opera­
tion in this study seemed somewhat arbitrary. But it did not affect the 
data interpretation because it was used to compare the critical flux of 
anaerobic sludge with and without microaeration while keeping biogas 
scouring (i.e., representative of crossflow velocity) and membrane the 
same. Thus, the critical flux zone was determined as 1.76–2.71 LMH and 
2.71–3.53 LMH for no microaeration and microaeration, respectively. 
As for the higher TMP increase rate under the highest flux tested 
(~3.4–3.5 LMH, already above critical flux) for anaerobic sludge with 
than without microaeration, it was reasonable because the TMP increase 
rate during super-critical flux filtration reflected the cake layer resis­
tance increase rate, which was affected by multiple factors of cake layer 
including thickness, porosity and compressibility (Field & Pearce, 
2011). Compared with anaerobic sludge without microaeration, anaer­
obic sludge with microaeration could have less amount of sludge flocs 
deposited onto membrane surface but might form cake layer with higher 
specific resistance, thus leading to a higher TMP increase rate. As a 
summary, microaeration showed consistent improvements on anaerobic 
sludge filterability for both starch and peptone feeding groups, which 
could be attributed to the effects of microaeration on anaerobic sludge 
characteristics below.

3.2.2. Particle size distribution and settleability of anaerobic sludge 
From sludge components analysis (see supplementary materials), for 
starch-feeding group, the easy-to-settle SS accounted for average 50.5 
%, 80.7 % and 62.8 % of total SS in AD1, AD2, and AD3, respectively, 
indicating a significant improvement of settling characteristics by 
microaeration. For peptone-feeding group, the easy-to-settle SS 
accounted for average 59.7 %, 63.1 % and 61.7 % of total SS in AD4, 
AD5, and AD6, respectively, indicating a small improvement of settling 
characteristics by microaeration. In addition, the higher proportion of 
easy-to-settle SS in AD3 and AD6 than in AD1 and AD4, respectively, 
could be derived from attenuation effects of microaeration in AD2 and 
AD5. Fig. 4 shows the particle size distribution of anaerobic sludge at the 
end of AD tests. From Fig. 4a and d, particle size distribution of anaer­
obic sludge showed a clear shift to larger size with average diameter 
increase from 33.5 to 43.8 µm and 34.3 to 58.7 µm after microaeration 
for starch-feeding group and peptone-feeding group, respectively, which 
could result in the proportion increase of easy-to-settle SS (see 
supplementary materials). According to the critical flux theory and the 
inertial lift model in crossflow filtration (Field & Pearce, 2011; Huang 
et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010), larger particles have higher lateral inertial 
lift velocity away from membrane surface and thus require higher 
permeation velocity (i.e., membrane flux) to make them deposited on 
membrane surface under the same crossflow conditions, resulting in 
higher critical flux for cake layer fouling formation. This could be the 
main mechanism behind the higher critical flux and thus better filter­
ability of anaerobic sludge with microaeration in Fig. 3. From Fig. 4b 
and c, both the easy-to-settle SS and the difficult-to-settle SS from starch- 
feeding group showed a significant shift to larger size with average 
diameter increase from 18.5 to 33.5 µm and from 15.3 to 30.0 µm after 
microaeration, respectively. From Fig. 4e and f, the easy-to-settle SS 
from peptone-feeding group showed significant shift to larger size with 
average diameter increase from 25.8 to 30.4 µm while the difficult-to- 
settle SS showed only marginal size shift with average diameter in­
crease from 0.882 to 0.988 µm after microaeration. Thus, the tendency

Previous studies on microaeration for AD mostly focused on bio­
logical performance. Only a few studies (Ruan et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 
2021) investigated the effects of microaeration on anaerobic sludge 
dewaterability and found that microaeration could increase particle size 
and enhance dewaterability. However, there is still no available infor­
mation on the effects of microaeration on anaerobic sludge filterability 
for AnMBR application so far in the literature. Although the particle size 
increase of anaerobic sludge induced by microaeration could provide 
solid supports for critical flux increase in this study, the deep mecha­
nisms should be further investigated via clarifying how microaeration 
would affect EPS secretion and the following anaerobic aggregation in 
the following studies. 
3.3. Effect of microaeration and substrate on microbial community and 
metabolism 
3.3.1. Genes abundance encoding enzymes for hydrolysis 
The total count of the sequencing data sets for Sludge-Blank, Sludge- 
Starch and Sludge-Peptone (see deposited raw data referring to acces­
sion number of SRR28311681, SRR28311682 and SRR28311683 in 
NCBI, respectively) was 27023382, 29,678,096 and 28393142, respec­
tively, showing the comparable levels among three samples in this study. 
The relative abundance (i.e., the count ratio of the specific gene to all 
genes) was employed for better comparison among the three samples. 
The abundance of genes encoding enzymes involved in hydrolysis of 
starch, glucose, and protein revealed the potential effects of microaer­
ation on hydrolysis (see supplementary materials). There was a 6.9 % 
and 6.7 % higher abundance of genes encoding enzymes involved in 
hydrolysis of starch and glucose in Sludge-Starch than in Sludge-Blank, 
respectively. Considering Sludge-Blank had been acclimated to soluble 
starch (i.e., dissolving the same insoluble starch used in this study in hot 
water of 70 ◦C) in AnMBR operation prior to this study, the higher 
abundance of genes encoding enzymes involved in hydrolysis of starch 
and glucose in Sludge-Starch could be induced by microaeration, 
showing the consistency with previous analyses on polysaccharide in 
Fig. 1a and demonstrating the enhanced hydrolysis by microaeration. 
There was a 23.3 % higher abundance of genes encoding ATP-dependent 
protease involved in hydrolysis of protein in Sludge-Peptone than in 
Sludge-Blank. Considering Sludge-Blank had not been acclimated to 
peptone, the higher abundance of genes encoding enzymes involved in 
hydrolysis of protein in Sludge-Peptone could be derived from both 
acclimation and microaeration. These results demonstrated that 
microaeration could enhance hydrolysis of polysaccharide and protein 
via promoting the secretion of hydrolase (Fu et al., 2022; Nguyen & 
Khanal, 2018). 
3.3.2. Species abundance at genus level 
Fig. 5a and b show the species abundance (at genus level) compar­
ison between Sludge-Starch and Sludge-Blank, and between Sludge- 
Peptone and Sludge-Blank. First of all, as a fast growing and produc­
ing propionic acid species under exclusively anaerobic conditions 
(Collograi et al., 2022), Propionibacterium showed an abundance of 1.3 
% in Sludge-Blank while dramatically decreased to an abundance of 
0.56 % and 0.00024 % in Sludge-Starch and Sludge-Peptone, respec­
tively. This could be derived from the inhibition of microaeration on 
Propionibacterium in Sludge-Starch and Sludge-Peptone, thus leading to 
lower abundance of Propionibacterium and propionic acid production, 
which was consistent with the previous results of VFAs in Fig. 2. These 
results demonstrated that microaeration could enhance AD performance 
via reducing Propionibacterium abundance and thus propionic acid 
production. 
From Fig. 5a, Mesotoga involved in acetate oxidation (Meng et al., 
2022), was enriched from the abundance of 1.21 % in Sludge-Blank 
(previously acclimated to soluble starch) to the abundance of 1.87 % 
in Sludge-Starch under microaeration. This could be ascribed into 
microaeration and result in the low acetic acid at the end of AD2 (shown 
in Fig. 4a). Desulfocurvus, which could facilitate the dissolution/hydro­
lysis of organics, degrade organics as iron reducing bacteria, and 
establish direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) with some metha­
nogens to improve methanogenic efficiency (Xu et al., 2020), was 
enriched from the abundance of 3.21 % in Sludge-Blank to the abun­
dance of 3.43 % in Sludge-Starch, indicating the enhanced AD perfor­
mance by microaeration. Sporosarcina mainly involved in fermentative 
acidification including acidogenesis and acetogenesis (Mahdy et al., 
2019; Thakur et al., 2024), was enriched from the abundance of 0.04 % 
in Sludge-Blank to the abundance of 5.01 % in Sludge-Starch, indicating 
the significantly enhanced fermentative acidification by microaeration. 
For methanogenic species, Methanothrix and Methanocorpusculum widely 
known to be involved in DIET (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2020), 
showed the abundance of 2.45 % and 0.58 % in Sludge-Blank and the 
abundance of 2.41 % and 0.68 % in Sludge-Starch, respectively, 
demonstrating that the microaeration did not only inhibit methanogens 
but also enrich methanogens via promoting dissolution/hydrolysis and 
DIET in this study. Considering Sludge-Blank had been acclimated to 
soluble starch for a long time prior to this study, it was reasonable that 
there was a similar microbial community structure between Sludge- 
Blank and Sludge-Starch. 
From Fig. 5b, the species involved in the hydrolysis/acidification of 
organics including Pseudomonas, Firmicutes, Clostridiaceae, Chloroflexi, 
Bacilli, and Clostridium (Gamble et al., 2011; Ye et al., 2017), were all 
enriched from the abundance of 0.07 %, 0.27 %, 0.53 %, 0.62 %, 0.01 %, 
0.13 % in Sludge-Blank to the abundance of 0.16 %, 1.47 %, 1.48 %, 
0.71 %, 3.69 %, 0.67 % in Sludge-Peptone, respectively. Proteiniphilum 
responsible for protein hydrolysis (Tao et al., 2023), was slightly 
enriched from the abundance of 0.44 % in Sludge-Blank to the abun­
dance of 0.46 % in Sludge-Peptone. Aminobacterium, which could 
oxidize amino acids (e.g., alanine, glutamate, leucine, isoleucine, valine, 
aspartate, and methionine) to produce formate for methanogenesis 
(Baena et al., 2000; Baena et al., 1998; Hamdi et al., 2015), was 
significantly enriched from the abundance of 1.98 % in Sludge-Blank to 
the abundance of 6.90 % in Sludge-Peptone. For methanogenic species, 
Methanothrix and Methanosarcina showed the abundance of 2.45 % and 
0.01 % in Sludge-Blank, and of 0.0012 % and 2.49 % in Sludge-Peptone, 
respectively, indicating a clear transition from dominant Methanothrix in 
Sludge-Blank to Methanosarcina in Sludge-Peptone. Methanothrix is 
known to use only acetic acid to produce methane, while Methanosarcina 
can achieve methane production using multiple substrates of methyl­
amine, methanol, hydrogen and acetic acid (Guo et al., 2015). This 
transition could be a reason for the higher methane production. 
Considering the Sludge-Blank had not been acclimated to peptone in this 
study, the significant difference of microbial community structure be­
tween Sludge-Blank and Sludge-Peptone could be derived from the ef­
fects of microaeration as well as substrate transfer from starch to 
peptone. 
Fig. 5c and d show the correlation network between environmental 
factors and species. Consistent with the abovementioned results, there 
was a positive correlation between microaeration and most facultative 
bacteria in Fig. 5c, which agreed well with some previous studies (Amin 
et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2022). However, there was a negative correlation 
between microaeration and some methanogens, indicating that 
microaeration was not actually favorable to the growth of methanogens. 
Therefore, the abundance increase of some methanogens in AD with 
microaeration in this study could be ascribed into 1) preventing 
methanogens from oxygen exposure via rapid oxygen consumption by 
facultative bacteria and formation of large layered particles (Nguyen & 
Khanal, 2018), and 2) providing sufficient substrates for methanogens 
via promoting dissolution/hydrolysis and DIET. In addition, microaer­
ation showed a positive effect on Proteiniphilum and Aminobacterium, 
which could be one of potential reasons for the enhance protein

3.3.3. Genes abundance involved in anaerobic metabolism 
Enrichment of functional flora usually increases metabolic activity. 
Fig. 6 presents the abundance of functional genes involved in glycolysis 
(Fig. 6a), amino acid metabolism (Fig. 6b), methane metabolism via 
acetate-type (Fig. 6c), carbon dioxide-type (Fig. 6d) and methyl 
compound-type (Fig. 6e). From Fig. 6a, Sludge-Starch showed the 12.2 
%, 2 %, 3.9 % higher abundance of PK, FBA, GPI, and the 5.43 %, 5.79 
%, 6.72 % lower abundance of ENO, PGK, pfkA, respectively, than 
Sludge-Blank, indicating the minor effects of microaeration on glycol­
ysis. Compared with Sludge-Blank, Sludge-Peptone showed the 211 %, 
74.6 %, 132.6 %, 576.3 %, 219.5 %, 177.7 % higher abundance of PK, 
PGAM, GAPDH, pfk, pfkA glk2, and the 96.9 %, 32 %, 125 % lower 
abundance of ENO, apgM, FBA, respectively, and absence of some genes 
(pfkB, glk, HK), indicating the major effects of substrate transfer from 
starch to peptone on glycolysis. From Fig. 6b, Sludge-Starch showed the 
1.87 % lower abundance of the functional genes involved in alanine (one 
of typical amino acids) metabolism than Sludge-Blank, which might be 
caused by the lack of amino acid source from the substrate. Sludge- 
Peptone showed the 338.5 % higher abundance of the functional 
genes involved in alanine metabolism than Sludge-Blank, which could 
be derived from substrate transfer from starch to peptone as well as 
microaeration, considering the positive correlation between microaer­
ation and Aminobacterium responsible for amino acids metabolism in 
Fig. 5c. 
From Fig. 6c, d, and e, Sludge-Blank, Sludge-Starch, Sludge-Peptone 
showed the abundance of 0.715 %, 0.743 %, 1.13 % for genes involved 
in the acetate-type methanogenic pathway, the abundance of 0.318 %, 
0.315 %, 0.503 % for genes involved in carbon dioxide-type methano­
genic pathway, and the abundance of 0.000808 %, 0.000504 %, 0.212 % 
for genes involved in methyl compound-type methanogenic pathway, 
respectively. The very low abundance of genes involved in methyl 
compound-type methanogenic pathway in Sludge-Blank and Sludge- 
Starch could be due to the lack of methyl compound (e.g., methyl­
amine) and its precursor (e.g., amino acid) caused by the lack of protein 
in the substrate (Guo et al., 2015), which was consistent with the low 
abundance of Methanosarcina in Sludge-Blank and Sludge-Starch in 
Fig. 5. The similar abundance of genes involved in the acetate-type and 
carbon dioxide-type methanogenic pathways between Sludge-Starch 
and Sludge-Blank indicated no obvious negative effects of microaera­
tion on methane metabolism. Sludge-Peptone showed the 261.1 % 
higher abundance of genes involved in methyl compound-type meth­
anogenic pathway than Sludge-Blank, indicating the strong effects of 
substrate transfer from starch to peptone on methane metabolism, which 
was consistent with the 248 % higher abundance of Methanosarcina in 
Sludge-Peptone than Sludge-Blank in Fig. 5. In addition, for all three 
samples, there was a descending order for the abundance of genes 
involved in the acetate-type, carbon dioxide-type, and methyl 
compound-type methanogenic pathways, indicating the dominant 
acetate-type and carbon dioxide-type methanogenic pathways in this 
study. 
4. Conclusions 
Bubble-free membrane microaeration was employed to enhance 
dissolution/ hydrolysis of insoluble/macromolecular organics and 
sludge filterability for AnMBR application. The batch AD tests feeding 
insoluble starch and soluble peptone with and without microaeration 
showed that microaeration increased methane production via promot­
ing 
dissolution/hydrolysis/acidification 
and 
critical 
flux 
of 
microfiltration membrane via driving large sludge flocs formation. The 
metagenomic analyses showed that microaeration enriched functional 
genes and bacteria for hydrolysis and acidification but showed little 
effect on functional genes for anaerobic metabolisms. The optimal ORP 
for microaeration-assisted AnMBR and evaluation of the promising 
microaeration method via bubble-free membrane or nanobubble are 
worthy of investigation.
